They are typically custom designed for specific applications. Design drivers include power and voltage ratings along with functional requirements such as generator step-up, industrial step-down, phase shift, or autotransformers. Hydropower plants require a generator step-up transformer to match transmission system voltages. The core-type LPT shown in Figure 1 is a typical configuration for generator step-up transformers. A hydropower facility may use a three-phase transformer, or three single-phase transformers. A three-phase transformer requires less material and costs less than an equivalent bank of three single-phase transformers; however, single-phase transformers have smaller dimensions and may be more suitable for sites with transportation constraints (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers 2024). 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Source: Office of Electricity Delivery and Energy Reliability (2014) The main components of transformers are the tank—which contains the core, windings, OLTC, and oil—bushings, oil conservator, and cooling system. The core and windings are the active electromagnetic components of the transformer; the OLTC adjusts the voltage ratio under varying load conditions; bushings provide insulated pathways for secure high-voltage electrical connections; and the oil-cooling system provides cooling and electrical insulation, maintaining dielectric strength and reducing overheating. Digital monitoring systems are included in modern LPTs to enhance durability and operational efficiency. Copper and electrical steel account for more than 50% of the total equipment cost. Transformer cores are primarily made from GOES (Chakraborty 2018). High magnetic permeability (Hi-B) grade electrical steel reduces losses and allows for the use of less material compared with lower grades of GOES. Continuously transposed conductors (CTCs) made from copper (or, less frequently, aluminum) are used in windings. Advancements in CTC manufacturing have improved voltage regulation, heat dissipation, and loss profiles. Cooling technology has also evolved. Traditional oil natural, air natural cooling has been supplemented or replaced in many applications by oil natural, air forced and oil forced, air forced systems, allowing for higher load capacities without overheating (USITC 2024a). In rehabilitation projects, upgrades to cooling systems are common, improving both performance and lifespan (Putsche et al. 2024). Insulating materials such as kraft paper, pressboard, or engineered polymers provide the necessary thermal and long-term dielectric stability for the service life of the transformer. Historically, cellulose-based paper was the dominant insulation medium, but newer designs incorporate aramid fibers and thermally upgraded paper, extending transformer life and improving thermal performance. 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Another notable trend is the shift from using traditional mineral oil to using synthetic or natural ester fluids as the insulating and cooling medium. These fluids have higher flash points than mineral oil, increasing fire safety.
